title: McGuffey's Sixth Eclectic Reader
sourceTitle: McGuffey's Sixth Eclectic Reader, Revised Edition
author: William Holmes McGuffey
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg eBook #16751: 'Public domain in the USA.' Revised edition first copyrighted 1879 (Van Antwerp, Bragg & Co.); renewals 1896 (American Book Company) and 1907 and 1921 (Henry H. Vail), all before 1930.
description: The last and richest McGuffey Reader: 138 selections from Shakespeare, Milton, Webster, Irving, Longfellow, Bryant, the Bible, and many more, opening with a short course in elocution. Each day your student learns a few hard words, reads a speech, story, or poem aloud with expression, then narrates it in speech or writing, or memorizes a stanza. A classic of American schooling, and the full text is free online.
includes: 145 lessons in 15 units: 7 elocution lessons plus all 138 Sixth Reader selections
Link to the free full text for every lesson
Key vocabulary, a read-aloud step, and a narration, written narration, or memory work each day
Parent notes on authors, historical context, and dated or sensitive content

lessons.title: Elocution: Articulation
steps: New words: articulation (clear speaking of sounds), vocals (pure vowel tones), subvocals (sounds mixing voice and breath, like b, d, v), aspirates (breath-only sounds, like p, t, f)
Read the explanation aloud, then say each sound in the Table of Vocals sharply, 'like the crack of a rifle'
Practice the 'Faults to Be Remedied' lists: say each word correctly, then hear how the careless version sounds
questions: Into what three groups does the book divide the elementary sounds?
Name two common faults of articulation.
What is a diphthong?
answers: Vocals, subvocals, and aspirates
Dropping or mis-sounding an unaccented vowel, dropping final consonants, skipping syllables, and running words together (any two)
Two vowel sounds joined in one, as in oil or now
lessons.notes: The book's introduction teaches elocution (reading aloud well). Spread these lessons over the first two weeks, and return to the drills all year.

lessons.title: Elocution: Inflection
steps: New words: inflection (a slide of the voice up or down), interrogative (asking a question), antithesis (a contrast of opposites), emphasis (special force on a word)
Read the explanation and say each example aloud, sliding your voice as marked
Learn Rules I–VIII: make up one sentence of your own for any three of them
questions: Which way does the voice slide at the end of a complete statement?
What inflection does a question answered by yes or no usually take?
What inflection do negative sentences usually take?
answers: Downward (falling inflection)
Rising
Rising
lessons.notes: The Gutenberg text shows inflection marks with plain apostrophes, so the rising and falling marks look alike. Use the rules and your ear.

lessons.title: Elocution: Series, Parenthesis, Circumflex, and Monotone
steps: New words: series (a list of words or phrases), parenthesis (words set apart within a sentence), circumflex (a voice slide that goes both up and down), monotone (one unchanging tone)
Read the rules and examples aloud, from 'Of Series' through 'Monotone'
Practice: read a list sentence of your own, then a sarcastic sentence using the circumflex
questions: How should a parenthesis be read?
What is the circumflex used to express?
When is the monotone used?
answers: More quickly and in a lower key than the rest of the sentence
Irony, sarcasm, supposition, or contrast
Mainly for grave, solemn, or awe-filled passages

lessons.title: Elocution: Accent and Emphasis
steps: New words: accent (stress on a syllable), absolute emphasis (stress not depending on a contrast), relative emphasis (stress that marks a contrast), emphatic pause (a pause that makes a word stand out)
Read the explanations and say each example aloud
Read one sentence three times, stressing a different word each time, and talk about how the meaning changes
questions: What is the difference between accent and emphasis?
Besides stress, name two other ways to give a word emphasis.
Is 'We can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth' an example of absolute or relative emphasis?
answers: Accent falls on a syllable within a word; emphasis falls on a word or phrase in a sentence
Lowering the voice (even to a whisper) or pausing before the word
Relative (it contrasts 'against' and 'for')

lessons.title: Elocution: Reading Verse
steps: New words: caesura (a pause near the middle of a line of poetry), poetic pause (a slight pause at the end of a line), simile (a comparison using like or as), sing-song (a chanting, rocking delivery)
Read the instructions and examples aloud
Choose a short poem you know and read it twice: once in a sing-song, once correctly with natural pauses
questions: What is the hardest thing about reading poetry aloud, according to the book?
What is the caesura?
How should a simile be read?
answers: Keeping its measured flow without falling into a chant
A pause at or near the middle of a line
In a lower key and a little faster, like a parenthesis

lessons.title: Elocution: The Voice
steps: New words: pitch (how high or low the voice is), compass (the voice's range), quantity (how long a sound is held), movement (speed of reading)
Read the explanations and examples for pitch, quantity, and movement aloud
Read one example passage slowly, one moderately, and one quickly, as the book suggests for each mood
questions: What is the natural pitch of the voice?
What is quantity in reading?
What fault does the book say most pupils have with movement?
answers: Its keynote, the pitch used in ordinary conversation
The length of time spent sounding a syllable or word
Reading too fast

lessons.title: Elocution: Gesture, and Elocution and Reading
steps: New words: gesture (movement of the body that adds meaning), attitude (posture), propriety (fitness, rightness), modulation (varying the voice)
Read the section on gesture and try its advice: stand tall, weight on one foot, open hand, free arm
Read 'Elocution and Reading' and the verses 'On Modulation' aloud
Copywork: “But none emphatic can that speaker call, / Who lays an equal emphasis on all.”
questions: What is the usual fault of young speakers in gesture?
Where does the book say training in good speaking must begin?
What happens if you put equal emphasis on every word?
answers: Too much action
In childhood, in the nursery
No word stands out; it is the same as no emphasis at all
lessons.notes: This ends the introduction. Keep coming back to these sections as your student reads the selections aloud.

lessons.title: Lesson I: Anecdote of the Duke of Newcastle
steps: New words: levees (morning receptions held by a great man), borough (a town that sends a member to Parliament), excise (a tax on goods; an exciseman collects it), post haste (as fast as possible)
Read the anecdote aloud, giving the Duke and the Cornish voter different voices
Narrate the story in order: the promise, the long wait, and the midnight mix-up
questions: What favor did the Cornish voter ask of the Duke?
Why did the Duke think the voter was a messenger?
What is the joke in the last line?
answers: That his son-in-law get the post of supervisor of excise when the old supervisor died
He was waiting up for news that the King of Spain had died, and had ordered his porter to send any messenger straight up
The Duke could not put the man on the throne of Spain, so he gave him the post he actually wanted: exciseman
lessons.notes: From Blackwood's Magazine. The Duke of Newcastle was a chief minister under George II; the King of Spain was Ferdinand VI.

lessons.title: Lesson II: The Needle
steps: New words: cotillon and quadrille (old dances), whist (a card game), talisman (a charm with magic power), rout (a large evening party)
Read the poem aloud, letting the repeated refrain ring each time
Copywork: “The bright little needle, the swift-flying needle”
questions: What does the poet prefer to dancing, painting, and music?
What line is repeated at the end of every stanza?
answers: A young woman who loves her home and is skilled with the needle
“The needle directed by beauty and art.”
lessons.notes: Poem by Samuel Woodworth. Its view of what makes a young woman admirable is very much of its time; a good chance to talk about how ideas of 'accomplishments' have changed.

lessons.title: Lesson III: Dawn
steps: New words: spectral (ghostly), zenith (the point straight overhead), concave (the curved bowl of the sky), Magians (ancient Persian sun and fire worshipers)
Read the short life of Edward Everett, then read the description aloud slowly, as if painting the sky with your voice
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe how the night sky changed into morning on Everett's train ride
Look out at dawn this week and find Jupiter or the Pleiades if they are visible
questions: Why was Everett up at two o'clock in the morning?
Which stars does he say went to rest first?
What amazed Everett more than the ancient sun worshipers?
answers: To catch the early train from Providence to Boston
The smaller stars, like little children
That people in his own day can watch the sunrise and still say there is no God
lessons.notes: By Edward Everett, from an address on the uses of astronomy. Point out the figures of speech in the third and fourth paragraphs.

lessons.title: Lesson IV: Description of a Storm
steps: New words: desolation (ruin), eddies (whirling currents), sluices (channels for water), firmament (the sky), cataract (a great waterfall)
Read the storm aloud, building speed and force through the long lists of sounds
Narrate: tell the storm in three stages, from the wind, to the silence, to the falling mountain
questions: What broke the sudden dead silence?
What made the mountain peak fall?
answers: Only the splash of the stirred-up lake against the rocks
A lake burst on its summit and the waterfall became a falling ocean
lessons.notes: By Benjamin Disraeli, novelist and later British prime minister. This is an excerpt from a novel, so the characters are not introduced.

lessons.title: Lesson V: After the Thunderstorm
steps: New words: tumultuous (wild and disorderly), azure (clear blue), kine (cattle), articulate (able to speak in words)
Read the poem aloud twice, the second time slowly enough to hear each picture
Memorize the first four lines, “As from the face of heaven the shattered clouds…”
questions: What sounds fill the fields after the storm?
Whom does the poet say ought to lead the hymn of thanks?
answers: Birdsong, cattle lowing, and sheep bleating
Man, who can speak words
lessons.notes: Poem by James Thomson, from 'The Seasons.'

lessons.title: Lesson VI: House Cleaning
steps: New words: prognostics (warning signs), scullion (a kitchen servant), testers (canopies over beds), wainscots (wooden panels on walls), pristine (original)
Read the essay aloud with a dry, mock-serious voice to bring out the humor
Written narration: in a paragraph, retell the whitewashing 'storm' from the point of view of the servant or the house
Make a list of the old-fashioned household words and what replaced them
questions: What sign tells the husband it is time to run?
How was the gentleman with the spoiled clothes 'doubly non-suited'?
What did the philosopher build, and did it work?
answers: A wheelbarrow of lime or buckets of whitewash in the yard
He lost both his suit of clothes and his lawsuit
A small room in the garden for the women to clean; no, it failed
lessons.notes: By Francis Hopkinson, a signer of the Declaration of Independence. It is satire; its jokes about 'female rage' belong to the 1700s, so talk about the humor and the way the target has aged.

lessons.title: Lesson VII: Schemes of Life Often Illusory
steps: New words: caliph (a Muslim ruler), viceroy (a governor ruling for a king), docility (willingness to be taught), connubial (of marriage), insatiable (never satisfied)
Read Omar's speech aloud as a wise old man talking to a young one
Written narration: list Omar's four plans and what actually happened to each
questions: What did Caleb ask Omar to teach him?
Why did Omar never travel?
What lesson does Omar give Caleb?
answers: The secret of how he gained his wisdom, power, and fortune
Business always kept him at court, and his presence was always needed
That it is of little use to form plans of life; time slips away
lessons.notes: By Samuel Johnson. An allegory in an Arabian Nights setting (Bagdad, the caliph's court).

lessons.title: Lesson VIII: The Brave Old Oak
steps: New words: renown (fame), rebec (an old stringed instrument), swains (country lads), hale (healthy)
Read the song aloud with a strong, steady beat
Memorize the first stanza
questions: What does the oak do on a wild midnight?
Who once gathered dew at the oak's feet?
answers: Shows his might as the storm shouts through his branches
Young maidens, on May Day
lessons.notes: Poem by Henry Fothergill Chorley. The 'ruthless king' is gold: the fear is that the oak will be cut down for ship timber.

lessons.title: Lesson IX: The Artist Surprised
steps: New words: propitiation (winning someone's favor), indefatigable (tireless), attenuation (thinness), thalers (old German silver coins)
Read the story aloud; let the auction bids grow louder as they climb
Narrate the story from Samuel's hidden nights of painting to the final check
questions: What did Samuel hope to get for his picture?
How much did the painting finally sell for?
What happened to Samuel after he became rich?
answers: Enough to buy food for about a week
One hundred thousand thalers
He lived richly but soon died of indigestion
lessons.notes: The author is not named. Albert Durer was a real German painter and engraver; Samuel's story is a tale, not history.

lessons.title: Lesson X: Pictures of Memory
steps: New words: gnarled (twisted and knotty), coquetting (flirting), cowslip (a yellow wildflower), immortal (never dying)
Read the poem aloud gently and slowly
Copywork: “Among the beautiful pictures / That hang on Memory's wall”
questions: Why is the old forest the best picture on Memory's wall?
What bed did the speaker make for her brother?
answers: Because her little brother is buried there
A bed of yellow leaves
lessons.notes: Poem by Alice Cary. It is about the death of a child, so read it first yourself if your child is sensitive.

lessons.title: Lesson XI: The Morning Oratorio
steps: New words: oratorio (a long musical work for voices), welkin (the sky), matin (morning), vermilion (bright red), subterranean (underground)
Read the essay aloud; pause after each bird is named and say what its song is like
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell the order in which the birds join the morning chorus
Go outside at dawn one morning this week and list the birds you hear first
questions: Which bird sings first and stops last?
What are the robins doing when they grow quiet?
How is the chorus different after sunrise?
answers: The hairbird (chipping sparrow)
Hopping on the ground hunting worms and insects for breakfast
It is more brilliant and lively but less continuous, and the bobolinks are loudest
lessons.notes: By Wilson Flagg, a New England nature writer. The 'hairbird' is the chipping sparrow.

lessons.title: Lesson XII: Short Selections in Poetry
steps: New words: emblem (a symbol), filches (steals), descries (sees, makes out), adorn (decorate, honor)
Read all six short poems aloud, one by one; say in a sentence what each is about
Memorize “My mind to me a kingdom is” (the stanza by William Byrd) or Shakespeare's “Good name in man or woman”
questions: In 'A Good Name,' why is stealing a good name worse than stealing a purse?
In 'Old Age and Death,' what lets new light into 'the soul's dark cottage'?
Who are the three poets in Dryden's lines on Milton?
answers: It does not make the thief richer but leaves the victim truly poor
The chinks (cracks) that time has made
Homer, Dante, and Milton
lessons.notes: Six short pieces: The Cloud (John Wilson), My Mind (William Byrd), A Good Name (Shakespeare, Othello), Sunrise (James Thomson), Old Age and Death (Edmund Waller), and Milton (John Dryden).

lessons.title: Lesson XIII: Death of Little Nell
steps: New words: languid (weak, limp), waning (fading), remorseless (without pity), decrepit (worn out with age), palsied (shaking, paralyzed)
Read the passage aloud quietly and slowly, with long pauses at the repeated words “She was dead”
Narrate: tell what Nell asked for, how she died, and how the little boy helped her grandfather
questions: What did Nell ask to have placed near her when she died?
What did she say often in her sleep?
How did the little boy help the old man?
answers: Something that had loved the light and had the sky above it always
“God bless you!”
His talk of Nell comforted him; he got him to rest and walk, and led him away when she was buried
lessons.notes: By Charles Dickens, from 'The Old Curiosity Shop' (1840). A famously sad scene about a child's death; preview it if your child is sensitive.

lessons.title: Lesson XIV: Vanity of Life
steps: New words: hireling (a hired worker), transgression (a sin, wrongdoing), iniquity (wickedness), countenance (face)
Read the poem aloud as a solemn lament
Open a Bible to Job 14 and compare a few lines with this translation
questions: What hope does a cut-down tree have that a man does not?
What questions does the speaker ask about death?
answers: It can sprout new shoots from its old root
Whether a man who dies shall live again, and where he is when he is taken away
lessons.notes: Herder's verse translation of Job 14, from his 'Hebrew Poetry.'

lessons.title: Lesson XV: A Political Pause
steps: New words: carnage (slaughter), implacable (unable to be calmed), expiring (dying), devastation (great destruction)
Read the speech aloud, making the sarcasm in “they are only pausing!” clear
Narrate: what did Fox think of calling the war a 'pause'?
questions: What word was Fox mocking?
What did the other side say the 'pause' was meant to test?
answers: “Pause” (a political pause in fighting)
Whether Bonaparte would behave better than before
lessons.notes: By Charles James Fox, from a speech against continuing the war with Napoleon's France. The book points out how a negative calls for a rising inflection here.

lessons.title: Lesson XVI: My Experience in Elocution
steps: New words: preceptor (teacher), obstreperous (noisy and unruly), aptitude (natural skill), depredations (raids; here, reading greedily)
Read the essay aloud; enjoy the lisping 'thunderbolths' line
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe Master Moody's way of teaching speaking and why Neal disliked it
questions: What nickname did Neal give the shy schoolmate?
What did Neal decide noises like stamping and thumping are not?
Who was the audience for Neal's first recitation?
answers: “O roarer” (from 'Aurora')
Oratory; untranslatable sounds are not language
His mother and sister
lessons.notes: By John Neal, an American writer from Portland, Maine.

lessons.title: Lesson XVII: Elegy in a Country Churchyard
steps: New words: curfew (evening bell), lea (meadow), glebe (soil), heraldry (family coats of arms), penury (poverty), sequestered (secluded)
Read the whole elegy aloud slowly, one stanza at a time
Memorize the first stanza, “The curfew tolls the knell of parting day…”
Copywork: “The paths of glory lead but to the grave.”
questions: Who is buried in the country churchyard?
What kept these villagers from becoming great?
What does the flower 'born to blush unseen' stand for?
answers: The poor, humble forefathers of the village
Poverty and lack of learning
Gifted people whose talents were never known to the world
lessons.notes: By Thomas Gray (1751), one of the best-known poems in English. Hampden, Milton, and Cromwell are explained in the notes.

lessons.title: Lesson XVIII: Tact and Talent
steps: New words: tact (the knack of saying and doing the right thing at the right time), momentum (force of motion), preferment (promotion), dexterously (skillfully)
Read the essay aloud, stressing each pair of opposites (talent is power, tact is skill…)
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain the difference between tact and talent, with an example from your own life
questions: Name two of the places where the author sets tact against talent.
According to the essay, which usually wins in practical life?
answers: The theater, the law courts (the bar), the church, the royal court, and the senate
Tact, “ten to one”
lessons.notes: The author is not named in the book. A good model of antithesis (balanced opposites).

lessons.title: Lesson XIX: Speech before the Virginia Convention
steps: New words: siren (a sea nymph who lured sailors to ruin), comports (fits, agrees), subjugation (conquest), remonstrated (protested), supinely (lying idle on one's back)
Read the life of Patrick Henry, then deliver the speech aloud, building to the last line
Memorize the final paragraph, from “Gentlemen may cry peace, peace…” to “give me liberty, or give me death.”
Written narration: in a paragraph, list Henry's reasons why the colonies must fight now
questions: What is the one lamp that guides Henry's feet?
What did Henry say the British fleets and armies were really meant for?
Why did he say waiting would not make the colonies stronger?
answers: The lamp of experience
To force the colonies into submission
Waiting would only let Britain disarm them and station a guard in every house
lessons.notes: By Patrick Henry, March 1775. Pair with a history of the opening of the Revolution. The book points to emphasis and the power of a pause or whisper in delivery.

lessons.title: Lesson XX: The American Flag
steps: New words: standard (a flag), baldric (a belt worn over the shoulder; here, the Milky Way), harbingers (signs of what is coming), welkin (the sky)
Read the poem aloud with energy and a strong rhythm
Memorize the first stanza, “When Freedom, from her mountain height…”
questions: Where did Freedom get the stars and stripes for the flag?
To whom does Freedom give the flag to guard?
answers: The stars from the night sky and the stripes from the morning light and the Milky Way
The eagle
lessons.notes: Poem by Joseph Rodman Drake. The battle imagery is vivid and glorifies war, as poems of its time often did.

lessons.title: Lesson XXI: Ironical Eulogy on Debt
steps: New words: ironical (saying the opposite of what is meant), eulogy (a speech of praise), duns (people demanding payment), regale (feast), extortioners (people who squeeze money out of others)
Read the essay aloud in a mock-serious voice, as if you truly believed it
Talk it over: what is the author really saying about debt and saving?
questions: Why is Mr. Payall unknown in his neighborhood?
What happens to the schoolboy who saves his plum cake?
Does the writer really think debt is good? How can you tell?
answers: He pays cash, so his name is in no one's account books
The others eat theirs, then rob and thrash him
No; it is irony, praising debt in absurd terms to show its folly
lessons.notes: The author is not named in the book. Explain irony before reading so the joke lands.

lessons.title: Lesson XXII: The Three Warnings
steps: New words: jocund (merry), delinquent (one who fails a duty), reprieve (a delay of punishment), fourscore (eighty), captious (quick to find fault)
Read the poem aloud, with a different voice for Death and for Dodson
Narrate the story of the bargain and how Death kept his word
questions: When did Death first come for Dodson?
What were the three warnings?
How old was Dodson when Death returned?
answers: On his wedding day
He became lame, blind, and deaf
Eighty (fourscore)
lessons.notes: Poem by Hester Lynch Thrale, friend of Samuel Johnson. A humorous fable about old age and death.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIII: The Memory of Our Fathers
steps: New words: veneration (deep respect), sedulously (carefully, busily), innovation (change), obloquy (blame, disgrace), bigotry (intolerance)
Read the address aloud as a preacher would
Written narration: in a paragraph, give Beecher's answer to people who mock the Puritan founders
questions: Why does Beecher think it dangerous to ridicule the founders?
What fault does he admit the founders had?
answers: Once their memory is despised, no one will value or keep up the institutions they built
They sometimes persecuted others
lessons.notes: By Lyman Beecher, a New England minister. This is a one-sided defense of the Puritans; his claim that other nations began as 'barbarians' and his praise of Puritan 'bigots' are worth discussing.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIV: Short Selections in Prose
steps: New words: antithesis (a contrast of opposites), adamantine (unbreakably hard), iris (the rainbow), ethereal (light and heavenly), evanescent (quickly fading)
Read the six short pieces aloud, one at a time; give each a one-line summary
Copywork: “Dryden is read with frequent astonishment, and Pope with perpetual delight.”
questions: In Johnson's comparison, whose writing is like a natural field and whose like a velvet lawn?
Whom is Las Casas begging not to fight?
According to Davy, what should we say instead of 'change' in nature?
answers: Dryden's is the natural field; Pope's the velvet lawn
Pizarro and his chieftains (the Spanish conquerors of Peru)
Progress
lessons.notes: Six pieces: Dryden and Pope (Samuel Johnson), Las Casas Dissuading from Battle (R. B. Sheridan), Action and Repose (John Ruskin), Time and Change (Sir Humphry Davy), The Poet (W. E. Channing), and Mountains (William Howitt).

lessons.title: Lesson XXV: The Jolly Old Pedagogue
steps: New words: pedagogue (schoolteacher), sallow (pale yellowish), Rule of Three (an old method for solving proportions), litigate (go to court), cronies (old friends)
Read the poem aloud with a warm, cheerful tone
Memorize the first stanza
questions: How did the old pedagogue feel about whipping?
How did he die?
answers: He thought it barbarous and seldom used the rod
Peacefully, sitting at his door on a midsummer evening
lessons.notes: Poem by George Arnold. The teacher enjoys 'a pipe and a friendly glass,' an ordinary pleasure in the 1860s.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVI: The Teacher and Sick Scholar
steps: New words: forms (long school benches), conning (studying, memorizing), impunity (freedom from punishment), lattice (a window of crisscrossed strips), chafing (rubbing to warm)
Read the chapter aloud; change pace from the noisy schoolroom to the quiet sickroom
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell how the schoolmaster's sorrow changed his school that day
questions: Whose copy did the master hold up as a model in writing time?
Why did the master give the boys a half holiday?
What did the sick boy ask the master to tie to the window?
answers: The sick scholar's
He could not keep his mind on lessons and wanted the village quiet for the sick child
His handkerchief, so the boys at play might see it and think of him
lessons.notes: From Charles Dickens's 'The Old Curiosity Shop.' The little scholar dies at the end; preview it for a sensitive child.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVII: The Snow Shower
steps: New words: prone (headlong), spangles (small glittering ornaments), burlier (bigger, heavier), myriads (huge numbers)
Read Bryant's life, then read the poem aloud, slowing on each “Flake after flake” refrain
Copywork: “Flake after flake / They sink in the dark and silent lake.”
questions: What do the paired snowflakes remind the poet of?
Why does the companion have a tear in her eye?
How does the poem end?
answers: Friends, or husband and wife, going through life hand in hand
She is thinking of dear friends who have died
The clouds part, a sunbeam falls, and the snow is gone, at rest in the lake
lessons.notes: Poem by William Cullen Bryant.

lessons.title: Lesson XXVIII: Character of Napoleon Bonaparte
steps: New words: prodigy (a wonder), despotic (like a tyrant), subaltern (a junior officer), immutable (unchangeable), vicissitudes (ups and downs of fortune)
Read the portrait aloud, giving weight to each balanced contrast
Written narration: in a paragraph, list three contradictions Phillips sees in Napoleon
questions: What does Phillips say Napoleon worshiped instead of God?
Name one way Napoleon acted against learning while pretending to favor it.
answers: Ambition
He jailed the press, banned books, persecuted authors, had the printer Palm shot, and banished Madame de Staël
lessons.notes: By Charles Phillips, an Irish orator. A one-sided, rhetorical portrait; the notes explain the many names.

lessons.title: Lesson XXIX: Napoleon at Rest
steps: New words: falchion (a curved sword), miters (bishops' hats), dirge (a funeral song), surge (rolling waves)
Read the poem aloud solemnly
Find St. Helena on a map and trace Napoleon's campaigns named in the first stanza (Egypt, the Alps, Moscow)
questions: Where is Napoleon buried in this poem?
What are the only sounds that mourn him?
answers: On the seagirt rock of St. Helena
The sea bird's cry, the surf, the clouds, and the wind
lessons.notes: Poem by John Pierpont. Napoleon's body was moved from St. Helena to Paris in 1840.

lessons.title: Lesson XXX: War
steps: New words: lurid (glaring, horrible), bereavement (loss of a loved one), wormwood and gall (bitter things), Golgotha (a place of skulls and death)
Read the address aloud; let the repeated answer ring out each time
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe one of Sumner's two scenes, the battlefield or the two ships
questions: What answer does Sumner give, twice, to 'wherefore this contest'?
What does he find more revolting than the wounded bodies?
answers: That this is the established method of deciding justice between nations
The lawless passions that sweep through the fight
lessons.notes: By Charles Sumner, from 'The True Grandeur of Nations' (1845). Graphic battlefield description; the notes explain Austerlitz, St. Bartholomew, and other references.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXI: Speech of Walpole in Reproof of Mr. Pitt
steps: New words: vehemence (great force of feeling), petulancy (peevishness), invective (abusive speech), epithets (labels, descriptive names), deference (respect)
Read the speech aloud in a cool, superior tone
Narrate: what does Walpole accuse young Pitt of?
questions: What does Walpole say young men should learn to do instead of declaiming?
What does he say is the difference between accusing and proving?
answers: To reason, and to prefer sound argument and facts to grand words
Reproaches without evidence only hurt the person who makes them
lessons.notes: By Sir Robert Walpole, prime minister of Great Britain. Read this and the next lesson as a pair.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXII: Pitt's Reply to Sir Robert Walpole
steps: New words: palliate (excuse), abhorrence (disgust), dissimulation (pretending), calumniator (a slanderer), supercilious (haughty)
Read the reply aloud with mounting indignation
Written narration: in a paragraph, say who won the exchange between Walpole and Pitt, and why
questions: What 'atrocious crime' does Pitt admit to?
When, says Pitt, does old age deserve contempt?
answers: Being a young man
When its years have passed without improvement and a man still blunders, or grows more wicked
lessons.notes: By William Pitt (later Earl of Chatham), the 'Great Commoner.'

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIII: Character of Mr. Pitt
steps: New words: chicanery (trickery), venal (open to bribes), posterity (future generations), subvert (overthrow)
Read the portrait aloud with dignity
Narrate: how did Pitt's speaking differ from Demosthenes's and Cicero's, according to Grattan?
questions: What were Pitt's object and his ambition?
How did Pitt unite a corrupt age?
answers: His object was England; his ambition was fame
Without corrupting anyone, by the force of his character
lessons.notes: By Henry Grattan, an Irish statesman.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIV: The Soldier's Rest
steps: New words: pibroch (bagpipe battle music), fallow (plowed but unplanted land), bittern (a marsh bird with a booming call), reveille (a wake-up call)
Read the song aloud softly, like a lullaby
Memorize the first stanza, “Soldier, rest! thy warfare o'er…”
questions: Who is being sung to sleep in the third stanza?
What gentle sounds may still be heard?
answers: A huntsman
The lark's song at daybreak and the bittern's booming
lessons.notes: Song by Sir Walter Scott, from 'The Lady of the Lake.'

lessons.title: Lesson XXXV: Henry V. to His Troops
steps: New words: breach (a gap broken in a wall), sinews (muscles and tendons), yeomen (common farmers serving as soldiers), mettle (courage, spirit)
Read Shakespeare's life, then declaim the speech aloud with fire
Memorize the opening, “Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more…”
questions: What animal should soldiers imitate in war?
What does Henry say his yeomen look like before the charge?
What is the battle cry?
answers: The tiger
Greyhounds straining at the leash
“God for Harry, England, and St. George!”
lessons.notes: From Shakespeare's 'King Henry V,' Act III, Scene 1, at the siege of Harfleur in France.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVI: Speech of Paul on Mars Hill
steps: New words: superstitious (here, very religious), offspring (children), Godhead (God's nature), Areopagite (a member of the court of the Areopagus)
Read the speech aloud as Paul would speak it to the Athenians
Compare with Acts 17:22–34 in your own Bible
questions: What altar inscription did Paul use to begin?
How did the Athenians respond?
answers: “To the Unknown God”
Some mocked, some wanted to hear more later, and a few believed, including Dionysius and Damaris
lessons.notes: From the Bible, Acts 17.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVII: God Is Everywhere
steps: New words: vault (an arched roof; here, the sky), orbs (heavenly bodies), immensity (vastness), finny nations (the fish of the sea)
Read the poem aloud as a dialogue: the first stanza asks, the others answer
Copywork: “The sun, the moon, the stars, his majesty declare.”
questions: What question does the first speaker ask?
Name the three places where the answer finds God.
answers: Where is God, and who is He?
The sky, the mountains, and the sea
lessons.notes: Poem by Joseph Hutton.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXVIII: Lafayette and Robert Raikes
steps: New words: pageant (a grand public show), jubilee (a great anniversary celebration), amaranthine (unfading), philanthropist (one who works for the good of others), lambent (softly glowing)
Read the address aloud; contrast the two imagined welcomes in your voice
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain why Grimké thought Raikes the greater benefactor. Do you agree?
questions: Who was Robert Raikes?
When did Lafayette revisit America?
How would Raikes's welcome have differed from Lafayette's?
answers: An English printer, the founder of Sunday schools
No cannons, parades, or balls; he would be welcomed by preachers, Sunday-school teachers, and children in churches
lessons.notes: By Thomas S. Grimké, from a Sunday-school address.

lessons.title: Lesson XXXIX: Fall of Cardinal Wolsey
steps: New words: wanton (playful, careless), Lucifer (the fallen angel), fortitude (strength to endure), inventory (a list of possessions)
Read the scene aloud with a partner, one taking Wolsey and the other Cromwell
Memorize from “Cromwell, I charge thee, fling away ambition” to “Corruption wins not more than honesty.”
questions: What does Wolsey compare a man's rise and fall to?
What news hurts Wolsey most?
What does Wolsey wish he had done differently?
answers: A plant that puts out leaves and blossoms, then is killed by frost
That Anne (Boleyn) has been seen in public as the king's queen
Served God with half the zeal he had served his king
lessons.notes: From Shakespeare's 'Henry VIII,' Act III, Scene 2. Cardinal Wolsey was Henry VIII's minister, disgraced in 1529.

lessons.title: Lesson XL: The Philosopher
steps: New words: embowered (sheltered by trees), sloven (untidy), anachronistical (out of its proper time), folios (large old books), residuum (what is left over)
Read the sketch aloud, enjoying the gentle humor
Narrate: describe Parson Chub, then tell what Ned found in the library at midnight
questions: Why did Parson Chub have to leave Ireland?
Why did Chub's plan for arranging the library fail?
What were Frank and the parson really doing in the library?
answers: He took part in the rebellion of 1798; his house was burned and his property seized
Several of his subject sections had no books at all
Sleeping over their books, with a pitcher of whisky punch
lessons.notes: By John P. Kennedy, from 'Swallow Barn,' sketches of plantation life in Virginia. The notes explain the many classical names.

lessons.title: Lesson XLI: Marmion and Douglas
steps: New words: behest (command), peer (an equal; a noble), portcullis (a heavy grated castle gate), rowels (spur points), gauntlet (an armored glove)
Read the notes first, then read the poem aloud with growing excitement at the chase
Memorize from “And dar'st thou then / To beard the lion in his den” to “Let the portcullis fall.”
questions: Why would Douglas not shake Marmion's hand?
How narrowly did Marmion escape?
What did Douglas admire about Marmion after all?
answers: Though he honored Marmion as the king's messenger, he despised his character
The falling gate grazed the plume of his helmet
He was bold in speech and a fine rider, a tried warrior
lessons.notes: By Sir Walter Scott, from 'Marmion.' Marmion is England's envoy at Tantallon Castle.

lessons.title: Lesson XLII: The Present
steps: New words: reverence (deep respect), monarch (a ruler), girt (surrounded), laurels (crowns of honor)
Read the poem aloud with conviction
Copywork: “Bids us serve the great To-day.”
questions: Who is the dead king, and who is the reigning queen, in this poem?
What will the Present do with the Past's promises?
answers: The Past is the dead king; the Present is the queen
Fulfill them
lessons.notes: Poem by Adelaide Anne Procter.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIII: The Baptism
steps: New words: kirk (church, in Scotland), chasm (a deep gorge), pellucid (crystal clear), sentinel (a lookout), Covenanters (Scottish Presbyterians who resisted the king's control of their church)
Read the story aloud; slow down for the gorge, speed up for the soldiers and the flood
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe the 'church' the Covenanters worshiped in
questions: Why did the congregation meet in a gorge and not in their kirk?
What signal warned them of danger?
What happened to the soldiers?
answers: It was a time of persecution; their worship was forbidden
A stone fell into the pool and a plaid was hung out on a shepherd's staff
A flash flood from a burst waterspout swept them away
lessons.notes: By John Wilson ('Christopher North'). Set during the persecution of the Scottish Covenanters in the 1600s; the soldiers' deaths are told as God's judgment.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIV: Sparrows
steps: New words: sires (fathers, ancestors), chitter (twitter), contrives (plans, arranges)
Read the poem aloud lightly, then again more thoughtfully for the last two stanzas
Copywork: “He planned for the birds, with the larger things.”
questions: What runs under the sparrows' feet without their knowing?
What does the poet compare to sparrows on God's telegraph strings?
answers: The news of the world, carried by the telegraph
The thoughts, works, and prayers of people, the little things in our lives
lessons.notes: Poem by Adeline D. T. Whitney. Explain the telegraph if needed.

lessons.title: Lesson XLV: Observance of the Sabbath
steps: New words: retribution (punishment for wrongdoing), auxiliaries (helpers), profligacy (reckless wickedness), profanation (treating something holy with disrespect), squalid (filthy and wretched)
Read the sermon aloud in a clear, earnest voice
Written narration: in a paragraph, list the good effects Spring says keeping the Sabbath has on a nation
questions: What does Spring call the Sabbath in his picture of an arch?
What did Lord Chief Justice Hale notice about the criminals he sentenced?
answers: The keystone of the arch that holds up the temple of virtue
Most said their wrongdoing began with neglecting the Sabbath
lessons.notes: By Gardiner Spring, a New York minister. A strongly argued sermon; his claims about Sabbath-breakers and prosperity are opinion, worth discussing.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVI: God's Goodness to Such as Fear Him
steps: New words: fret (worry), iniquity (wickedness), inherit (receive as one's own), bay tree (a spreading evergreen)
Read the psalm aloud slowly and reverently
Memorize “Trust in the Lord, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed.”
questions: Who shall inherit the earth, according to the psalm?
What has the old speaker never seen?
answers: The meek (those who wait upon the Lord)
The righteous forsaken, or his children begging bread
lessons.notes: From Psalm 37.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVII: Character of Columbus
steps: New words: commensurate (equal in size), magnanimity (generosity of spirit), irascible (quick-tempered), seditions (revolts), opulent (wealthy)
Read Irving's portrait aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe Columbus's character as Irving saw it, and one thing Columbus never knew about his discovery
questions: Whom does Irving blame for Columbus's failure to build orderly colonies?
What did Columbus believe he had found, to the end of his life?
answers: The unruly rabble he had to command
A new route to the rich lands of the East (Asia)
lessons.notes: By Washington Irving, from his 'Life and Voyages of Columbus.' Irving's admiring portrait leaves out Columbus's harsh treatment of the native peoples; older students can compare it with a modern account.

lessons.title: Lesson XLVIII: "He Giveth His Beloved Sleep"
steps: New words: undisproved (not shown false), overweep (weep over), delved (dug), mummers (costumed actors)
Read Psalm 127:2, then read the poem aloud quietly
Copywork: the refrain “He giveth his beloved, sleep.”
questions: What gifts might we wish to give the people we love?
What does God give instead?
answers: A hero's courage, a poet's harp, a patriot's voice, a king's crown
Sleep, peaceful rest
lessons.notes: Poem by Elizabeth Barrett Browning, built on Psalm 127:2. 'Sleep' here also means the rest of death.

lessons.title: Lesson XLIX: Description of a Siege
steps: New words: ensign (a flag), craven (coward), barbacan (a fortified outwork guarding a gate), palisades (fences of stakes), postern (a small back gate)
Read the notes on castles first, then read the scene aloud with two voices, Rebecca and Ivanhoe
Draw a castle with keep, walls, moat, barbacan, and postern gate
questions: Why can Ivanhoe not see the battle himself?
Who falls in the fight on the breach?
Whom does Ivanhoe guess the Black Knight to be?
answers: He is wounded and lying on a couch
Front de Boeuf
King Richard the Lion-Hearted
lessons.notes: By Sir Walter Scott, from 'Ivanhoe.' Rebecca's horror at the bloodshed is a good discussion point.

lessons.title: Lesson L: Marco Bozzaris
steps: New words: suppliance (humble begging), signet (a seal ring), Suliote (from the Suli Mountains of Greece), pestilence (a deadly plague), knell (a funeral bell)
Read the poem aloud, with a rousing voice for Bozzaris's battle cry
Memorize Bozzaris's cheer, from “Strike—till the last armed foe expires” to “God—and your native land!”
questions: What was the Turk dreaming about?
Who won the battle, and what happened to Bozzaris?
How does Death sound to the hero, unlike to others?
answers: Conquering Greece and sitting on his monarch's throne
The Greeks won, but Bozzaris was killed
Like a prophet's word, carrying the thanks of millions yet to be
lessons.notes: Poem by Fitz-Greene Halleck about the Greek war of independence against the Ottoman Turks (1823).

lessons.title: Lesson LI: Song of the Greek Bard
steps: New words: bard (a poet-singer), lay (a song), degenerate (decline), phalanx (a close battle formation), Bacchanal (a reveler)
Read the notes, then read the song aloud; find Marathon, Salamis, and Thermopylae on a map of Greece
Memorize the stanza beginning “The mountains look on Marathon”
questions: What does the bard mean by 'all, except their sun, is set'?
Why does he keep calling to 'dash down' the wine?
What does the bard ask the earth to give back?
answers: Greece's glory is gone; only its sunny climate remains
Drinking and dancing are a shameful escape from fighting for freedom
Three of the three hundred Spartans who died at Thermopylae
lessons.notes: By Lord Byron, from 'Don Juan' ('The Isles of Greece'). Byron died helping the Greeks fight for independence; the book's sketch of his life is frank about his faults.

lessons.title: Lesson LII: North American Indians
steps: New words: embellishes (decorates), sedgy (grassy, marshy), progenitors (ancestors), chronicles (written histories), exterminators (destroyers)
Read the address aloud with feeling
Talk it over: what does Sprague get right about what happened to Native peoples, and what does he get wrong in his view of them?
questions: What two kinds of seeds did the pilgrim ship bring, according to Sprague?
What does Sprague ask of those who write about the Indians' fate?
answers: Seeds of life (for the settlers) and of death (for the native peoples)
To be faithful to their virtues and pay due tribute to their unhappy fate
lessons.notes: By Charles Sprague, Fourth of July address, Boston, 1825. Parent note: the speech mourns Native Americans but calls them 'ignorant' and 'the poor child of nature' and wrongly assumes they would vanish. Native nations are very much alive today; a good chance to discuss this.

lessons.title: Lesson LIII: Lochiel's Warning
steps: New words: seer (a prophet), array (battle order), dotard (a foolish old man), claymore (a Scottish broadsword), fagots (bundles of sticks for burning)
Read the notes, then read the poem aloud as a dialogue between the Seer and Lochiel
Memorize the line “And coming events cast their shadows before,” and use it in a sentence of your own
questions: What battle does the Seer foresee?
Who wins it?
What does Lochiel vow at the end?
answers: Culloden (1746)
The English under the Duke of Cumberland; the Highlanders are routed
Never to flee or be taken; to fight or die with his feet to the foe
lessons.notes: Poem by Thomas Campbell, about the Jacobite rising for Charles Stuart ('Bonnie Prince Charlie').

lessons.title: Lesson LIV: On Happiness of Temper
steps: New words: disposed (inclined in mood), constitution (natural makeup), poignant (sharp, keen), construed (interpreted), sharper (a swindler), halter (a rope noose)
Read the essay aloud; enjoy the joke at the end
Written narration: in a paragraph, retell one of Goldsmith's examples of a happy temper and say whether you think he is right
questions: What did Cardinal de Retz do while in prison?
What did Dick's father leave him?
How did Dick answer?
answers: Laughed at his troubles and wrote the life of his jailer
A shilling to buy a halter (a rope to hang himself)
“May heaven give you life and health to enjoy it yourself!”
lessons.notes: By Oliver Goldsmith. The opening example, a chained and maimed slave who seems merry, treats slavery lightly; worth discussing.

lessons.title: Lesson LV: The Fortune Teller
steps: New words: russet (reddish brown), wag (a joker), alms (charity), intelligencers (informers), stewardship (managing money for another)
Read the story aloud, with a cheerful, sly voice for the beggar
Narrate: how did the beggar become a fortune teller, and how does he gather his 'fortunes'?
questions: Why did the beggar give up telling the truth about his misfortunes?
How does he learn things to tell people?
What did the dog do with Harley's shilling?
answers: People did not believe him or give him money without visible proof such as a wooden leg
He picks up names and gossip from servants and neighbors, and people tell him themselves
Snapped it up and gave it straight to his master
lessons.notes: By Henry Mackenzie, from 'The Man of Feeling.'

lessons.title: Lesson LVI: Rienzi's Address to the Romans
steps: New words: thraldom (slavery, bondage), feudal (ruled by lords over their lands), rapine (plunder), limners (painters), distained (stained, dishonored)
Read the notes, then deliver the speech aloud with rising passion
Practice the speech for inflection and emphasis, as the book suggests
questions: What are the Romans slaves to, according to Rienzi?
What personal wrong spurred Rienzi to call for vengeance?
What does Rienzi swear at the end?
answers: Petty tyrants and feudal lords
His gentle young brother was killed
That Rome shall be free again
lessons.notes: From Mary Russell Mitford's play 'Rienzi.' Cola di Rienzi led a revolt against Rome's nobles in 1347.

lessons.title: Lesson LVII: Character of the Puritan Fathers of New England
steps: New words: allegorized (shown as a symbol or story), unalienable (unable to be taken away), theocratical (ruled by religious law), ecclesiastical (of the church), Pentateuch (the first five books of the Bible)
Read the essay aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain how Greenwood says the Revolution grew out of the Puritans' homes
questions: How was the Puritans' view of liberty different from the ancients'?
Where was every settler's 'school of independence'?
How did the Puritans get their name?
answers: They did not make it a goddess; they held it as a birthright from the Creator
At his own hearth (fireside)
From their strict purity of manners and speech; it was first given in mockery
lessons.notes: By F. W. P. Greenwood. A warm defense of the Puritans that passes over their intolerance of dissenters (compare Lesson XXIII).

lessons.title: Lesson LVIII: Landing of the Pilgrim Fathers
steps: New words: bark (a ship), exiles (people forced from home), hoary (gray with age), shrine (a holy place)
Read the poem aloud, steady and strong
Memorize the whole poem, a few stanzas a day this week
questions: How did the Pilgrims NOT come, according to the poem?
What did they seek in the new land?
answers: Not as conquerors with drums and trumpets, nor as frightened fugitives
A faith's pure shrine: freedom to worship God
lessons.notes: Poem by Felicia Hemans. The Pilgrims landed at Plymouth in December 1620.

lessons.title: Lesson LIX: Necessity of Education
steps: New words: inexorable (unstoppable), perpetuity (lasting forever), suffrage (the right to vote), foundering (sinking), imminence (closeness of danger)
Read the address aloud, giving force to the opening cry
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain why Beecher thought the West needed schools and churches quickly
questions: What does Beecher say will happen if we do not educate?
Why is the fear of patriots 'the star of hope'?
answers: We will perish by our own prosperity
Fear stirs people to act, like wind that keeps a ship from foundering
lessons.notes: By Lyman Beecher, a plea for schools and churches in the growing West of the 1830s.

lessons.title: Lesson LX: Riding on a Snowplow
steps: New words: Cyclops (a one-eyed giant), windlass (a winch), momentum (force of motion), landlubber (a person unused to the sea)
Read the sketch aloud with lively expression
Narrate the trip from Buffalo to Erie as if you had been the passenger
questions: How many engines pushed the snowplow?
Why did the plow back up before each big drift?
What did the author resolve at the end?
answers: Three
To get a running start and momentum for a hard blow
Never again to 'ride a hammer' when three engines held the handle
lessons.notes: By Benjamin F. Taylor. A humorous travel sketch of an early railroad snowplow.

lessons.title: Lesson LXI: The Quarrel of Brutus and Cassius
steps: New words: itching palm (greed for bribes), choler (anger), testy (irritable), drachmas (Greek coins), indirection (dishonest means)
Read the notes on the Ides of March, then read the scene aloud with a partner
Narrate: what started the quarrel, and how was it made up?
questions: What does Brutus accuse Cassius of?
Why does Brutus say he could not raise money himself?
How does the quarrel end?
answers: Having an 'itching palm,' selling offices for gold, and refusing him money
He would not take it from peasants by dishonest means
They are reconciled and clasp hands; Brutus forgives Cassius's hot temper
lessons.notes: From Shakespeare's 'Julius Caesar,' Act IV, Scene 3. This is the scene John Neal mocked the lisping boys for performing in Lesson XVI.

lessons.title: Lesson LXII: The Quack
steps: New words: quack (a fake doctor), phlebotomize (bleed a patient), farrier (a horse doctor), pilchard (a small fish), Pandora (in Greek myth, the woman who opened the box of evils)
Read the scene aloud with three voices: Hostess, Lampedo, and Balthazar
Narrate: why were the hostess and the quack keeping Balthazar sick?
questions: Why did the hostess want Balthazar kept another fortnight?
What did Balthazar make Lampedo do as punishment?
How did the hostess 'ease her conscience' about her bad wine?
answers: To keep earning money from his stay at her inn
Swallow his own pills
By always giving short measure
lessons.notes: By John Tobin, from the comedy 'The Honeymoon.' Old medicine like bleeding is part of the joke.

lessons.title: Lesson LXIII: Rip Van Winkle
steps: New words: grizzled (gray-streaked), akimbo (hands on hips), austere (stern), tory (a supporter of the king), precipitation (great haste)
Read the note first to learn how Rip fell asleep, then read the scene aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell the story of Rip's return in your own words
questions: Why did the crowd shout 'A tory! a spy!'?
How did Rip finally learn who he was?
How long had Rip been asleep?
answers: He called himself a loyal subject of the king, after the Revolution
Through his grown daughter, Judith Gardenier, and an old woman who recognized him
Twenty years
lessons.notes: By Washington Irving, from 'The Sketch Book.' Read the whole story aloud if you can; the book's note calls Rip a drunkard, and the jab about his wife's death is old-fashioned humor.

lessons.title: Lesson LXIV: Bill and Joe
steps: New words: comrade (friend), ermined (trimmed with fur, as a judge's robe), chaffing (teasing), hic jacet (Latin: here lies)
Read the poem aloud warmly, as one old friend to another
Memorize the first stanza
questions: What honors has Bill won?
What does Holmes say fame is like?
What do Bill and Joe care about more than tombstones?
answers: Titles like Hon. and LL.D., a judge's robe, worldwide fame
A flickering flame, or a gust of wind that lifts a pinch of dust
Being remembered in the hearts of those who love them
lessons.notes: Poem by Oliver Wendell Holmes, written for his college classmates.

lessons.title: Lesson LXV: Sorrow for the Dead
steps: New words: attributes (qualities), compunctious (regretful), assiduities (careful attentions), unrequited (not repaid), chaplet (a wreath)
Read the essay aloud slowly
Written narration: in a paragraph, give Irving's lesson at the end and how you could act on it this week
questions: Why does Irving call this the one sorrow we do not want healed?
What lesson does he draw for how we treat the living?
answers: Because remembering the dead is a form of love we cherish
Be more faithful and loving to the living while we can
lessons.notes: By Washington Irving, from 'The Sketch Book.'

lessons.title: Lesson LXVI: The Eagle
steps: New words: beetling (overhanging), imperial (of an empire), legions (Roman armies), clarions (trumpets), deluge (flood)
Read the poem aloud with a sweeping rhythm
Copywork: “Bird of the broad and sweeping wing! / Thy home is high in heaven”
questions: What did the Roman legions carry the eagle on?
What was the 'one awful hour'?
answers: Their standards (the eagle was the Roman battle standard)
The fall of Rome to the northern barbarians
lessons.notes: Poem by James Gates Percival.

lessons.title: Lesson LXVII: Political Toleration
steps: New words: toleration (allowing views you disagree with), minority (the smaller group), countenance (approve, allow), theoretic (based on theory, not fact)
Read Jefferson's words aloud as an inaugural address
Memorize “We are all Republicans; we are all Federalists.” and talk about what it means
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain Jefferson's 'sacred principle' about the majority and the minority
questions: What must the will of the majority be, to be rightful?
Why does Jefferson let those who would dissolve the Union 'stand undisturbed'?
Why does he think this the strongest government on earth?
answers: Reasonable, and it must protect the equal rights of the minority
Error of opinion is safe when reason is left free to combat it
Every citizen would rally to the law and treat attacks on public order as his own concern
lessons.notes: From Thomas Jefferson's First Inaugural Address (1801), after the bitter election of 1800.

lessons.title: Lesson LXVIII: What Constitutes a State?
steps: New words: constitutes (makes up), battlement (a castle wall), endued (gifted), sovereign (supreme), empress (a female ruler)
Read the poem aloud as a question and answer
Memorize the second stanza, beginning “No:—men, high-minded men”
questions: Name two things the poet says do NOT make a state.
What does make a state?
answers: Walls, battlements, proud cities, harbors and navies, or glittering courts
High-minded people who know their duties and their rights, ruled by law
lessons.notes: Poem by Sir William Jones.

lessons.title: Lesson LXIX: The Brave at Home
steps: New words: sash (a band worn across the body), dissembles (hides), girds (fastens on), asunder (apart)
Read the poem aloud tenderly
Copywork: the last four lines of any stanza
questions: Which three women does the poem honor?
What does the poet say their hidden tears are equal to?
answers: The maid, the wife, and the mother who send their men to war
The blood shed by soldiers on the field of battle
lessons.notes: Poem by Thomas Buchanan Read, from 'The Wagoner of the Alleghanies.'

lessons.title: Lesson LXX: South Carolina
steps: New words: zealous (eager and devoted), adversity (hard times), filial (as a child to a parent), whigs (American patriots in the Revolution), invincible (unconquerable)
Read the speech aloud with pride, as a senator defending his state
Narrate: what does Hayne say South Carolina did in the Revolution?
questions: What does Hayne claim about South Carolina's devotion to the Union?
Which two Revolutionary leaders does he name?
answers: That no state has been more devoted or made greater sacrifices
Sumter and Marion
lessons.notes: By Robert Y. Hayne, from his 1830 Senate debate with Daniel Webster. Hayne was a leading defender of 'states' rights' and nullification, ideas later tied to the defense of slavery and secession. Read with the next lesson, Webster's reply.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXI: Massachusetts and South Carolina
steps: New words: eulogium (praise), circumscribed (fenced in, limited), gangrened (rotted, poisoned), tithe (a tenth; a tiny bit), encomium (formal praise)
Read Webster's life, then deliver the reply aloud with dignity
Memorize from “There is Boston, and Concord, and Lexington, and Bunker Hill” to “there they will remain forever.”
Written narration: in a paragraph, compare how Hayne and Webster each spoke about their states and the Union
questions: Why does Webster claim South Carolina's heroes as his own?
What does Webster say Massachusetts needs instead of praise?
Where does he say liberty would fall, if it must fall?
answers: They are Americans all; their fame belongs to the whole country, not one state
Nothing; just look at her history: Boston, Concord, Lexington, Bunker Hill
Beside its own cradle, on the very spot where it was born
lessons.notes: By Daniel Webster, from his 1830 reply to Hayne, one of the most famous speeches in Senate history.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXII: The Church Scene from Evangeline
steps: New words: sonorous (deep and loud), dissonant (harsh-sounding), forfeited (taken away as a penalty), imprecations (curses), tocsin (an alarm bell)
Read the note on the Acadians, then read the scene aloud in its long, rolling lines
Narrate: tell what the commander announced and how Father Felician calmed the people
questions: What did the king's order take from the Acadians?
Who shouted against the English and was struck down?
What prayer did Father Felician lead?
answers: Their lands, homes, and cattle; and they were to be sent away from the province
Basil the blacksmith
“O Father, forgive them!”
lessons.notes: From Longfellow's 'Evangeline' (1847), about the expulsion of the French Acadians from Nova Scotia in 1755. Find Nova Scotia on a map.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIII: Song of the Shirt
steps: New words: dolorous (sorrowful), gusset (a piece sewn in to strengthen a seam), respite (a short rest), briny (salty)
Read the poem aloud, letting “Work! work! work!” sound tired and heavy
Copywork: “O God! that bread should be so dear, / And flesh and blood so cheap!”
Talk about what Hood wanted his readers to do
questions: What is the woman really sewing besides a shirt?
What are her wages?
What does she long for, just for one hour?
answers: Her own shroud; the work is killing her
A bed of straw, a crust of bread, and rags
To breathe fresh air among flowers, with sky above and grass beneath
lessons.notes: Poem by Thomas Hood (1843), written to protest the treatment of London's seamstresses. The line about the 'barbarous Turk' reflects old prejudice.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIV: Diamond Cut Diamond
steps: New words: cadi (a Muslim judge), Banian (a Hindu merchant), ruse (a trick), piaster (a Turkish coin), pasha (a Turkish governor)
Read the story aloud; pause before each clever answer
Narrate the two cases and how Omar won each
questions: What payment did Omar demand from Ali the jeweler?
How did Omar answer his father's claim on the casket?
How did the cadi settle the second case?
answers: Twenty pounds of winged ants' wings, half male and half female
He offered a coin stamped with the sultan's face; refusing it would insult the ruler
The Banian was to pay Mansour a hundred thousand piasters, the worth of the necklace
lessons.notes: Adapted from 'Abdallah' by Édouard Laboulaye. The description of the young Banian is a dated stereotype.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXV: Thanatopsis
steps: New words: thanatopsis (a view of death), communion (close sharing), sepulcher (a tomb), patriarchs (founding fathers), quarry slave (a slave working in a stone quarry)
Read the poem aloud slowly; mark where the 'still voice' of Nature begins
Memorize the closing lines, from “So live, that when thy summons comes” to the end
questions: What does Nature do for us in our dark thoughts?
Why does Bryant say we will not lie down alone?
How should we approach our grave, according to the last lines?
answers: She steals away their sharpness with healing sympathy
All the great and good of past ages, and everyone who lives, lie in the same great tomb
Sustained by trust, like someone lying down to pleasant dreams
lessons.notes: Poem by William Cullen Bryant, begun when he was about seventeen.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVI: Indian Jugglers
steps: New words: ingenuity (cleverness), dexterity (skill with the hands), lambent (flickering), pliancy (flexibility), fastidious (hard to please)
Read the essay aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain why the juggler made Hazlitt think less of his own work. Is he fair to himself?
questions: How many balls could the juggler keep up?
Which feat did Hazlitt think the police should stop?
What does Hazlitt say his own essays lack that the juggler has?
answers: Four
Sword swallowing
Exact, flawless perfection that no one can find fault with
lessons.notes: By William Hazlitt, from 'Table Talk.' 'Indian' here means from India.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVII: Antony over Caesar's Dead Body
steps: New words: interred (buried), coffers (treasure chests), mutiny (revolt), testament (a will), vesture (clothing)
Read the notes, then deliver the speech aloud, watching how 'honorable' changes in meaning each time
Memorize the opening, from “Friends, Romans, countrymen” to “So let it be with Caesar.”
questions: What three things does Antony give as proof Caesar was not ambitious?
How does Antony make the crowd want to hear the will?
What did the crowd cry out at the end?
answers: He filled the treasury with ransoms, wept for the poor, and refused the crown three times
He keeps saying he must not read it, which makes them demand it
For revenge on the conspirators: “Burn! Fire! Kill! Slay!”
lessons.notes: From Shakespeare's 'Julius Caesar,' Act III, Scene 2. A master class in irony and persuasion.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXVIII: The English Character
steps: New words: aristocracy (the noble class), tenantry (tenant farmers), Nimrod (a mighty hunter), arrogance (pride that looks down on others), John Bull (a nickname for the typical Englishman)
Read the essay aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, list the good qualities and the faults Prescott found in the English
questions: Where, says Prescott, is the Englishman seen at his best?
What fault makes the Englishman unpopular abroad?
What does Prescott mean by 'The body travels, not the mind'?
answers: In his country home, at his fireside and farm
His air of national superiority, his arrogance
English travelers go everywhere but come home with their ideas and prejudices unchanged
lessons.notes: By William H. Prescott, the historian, from a letter written while visiting England. Some remarks (on women, on 'Hottentots,' on the 'superficial Frenchman') are broad stereotypes of his era.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXIX: The Song of the Potter
steps: New words: marl (a clay-rich soil), wax and wane (grow and shrink), kindred (related by birth), potsherds (broken pieces of pottery)
Read the poem aloud with a turning, even rhythm like a potter's wheel
Memorize the stanza beginning “Turn, turn, my wheel! The human race”
questions: What lesson does the potter draw from the clay?
What does the furnace flame do to the vessels?
answers: All people, whatever their rank or race, are made of the same clay and are kin
Tests them and stamps them with honor or shame
lessons.notes: Poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, from 'Kéramos.'

lessons.title: Lesson LXXX: A Hot Day in New York
steps: New words: labyrinth (a maze), languor (weakness, listlessness), truculence (fierceness), somnambulist (sleepwalker), apothecary (druggist)
Read the scene aloud; let your voice sound heavy with the heat
Narrate: describe the man with sunstroke in the drugstore and how he was treated
questions: What did the thermometer at the drugstore door read?
How was the sunstruck man being cooled?
Why does Basil say he would rather have an accident in New York?
answers: Ninety-seven degrees
His wife rubbed his head with a handkerchief full of pounded ice
The biggest place is both the cruelest and the kindest; there a good Samaritan is sure to be near
lessons.notes: By William Dean Howells, from the novel 'Their Wedding Journey.' 'Stages' were horse-drawn omnibuses.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXI: Discontent.—An Allegory
steps: New words: allegory (a story with a hidden meaning), ruminating (thinking over), chimerical (imaginary), fardel (a bundle), commodious (convenient)
Read the allegory aloud; picture the mountain of troubles
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell what happened when people swapped their troubles, and Addison's lesson
questions: Who led each mortal to the heap of troubles?
What did no one throw on the heap?
Who made the heap shrink, and how big did it become?
answers: Fancy, carrying a magnifying glass
A single vice or folly
Patience; it shrank to less than a third of its size
lessons.notes: By Joseph Addison, from 'The Spectator.' One man throws down 'his wife' as a burden, an old joke.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXII: Jupiter and Ten
steps: New words: portly (stout), sagacious (wise; used here as a joke), patron (a supporter), Lempriere (an old dictionary of mythology)
Read the poem aloud and save the surprise for the last line
Write the title as Mrs. Chub read it and as it really was; explain the mix-up
questions: What did Mrs. Chub say her painting was called?
What was its real title?
answers: Jupiter and Ten
Jupiter and Io (she misread 'Io' as the number 10)
lessons.notes: Humorous poem by James T. Fields, poking fun at people who show off a learning they do not have.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXIII: Scene from "The Poor Gentleman"
steps: New words: baronet (a British title below a lord), valet (a man's personal servant), flummery (empty flattery), syllogism (a three-step logical argument), indigence (poverty)
Read the scene aloud with three readers: Sir Robert, Humphrey, and Frederic
Narrate: what kind of man is Sir Robert under his gruffness?
questions: Why does Humphrey answer Sir Robert's question with only 'Hem'?
Why did Sir Robert quarrel with his brother Job?
What does Frederic rush off to do at the end?
answers: If he contradicts him he lies, and if he agrees Sir Robert picks a fight
Job was so meek he never argued back
To visit and help Lieutenant Worthington, the poor disabled officer
lessons.notes: From George Colman's comedy 'The Poor Gentleman.'

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXIV: My Mother's Picture
steps: New words: maternal (motherly), beguiled (fooled), dupe (one who is easily fooled), contemplation (quiet thought)
Read Cowper's life, then read the poem aloud gently
Copywork: “Oh that those lips had language! Life has passed / With me but roughly since I heard them last.”
questions: How old was Cowper when his mother died?
What did the maids promise the little boy?
What does Cowper boast of instead of noble birth?
answers: Six years old
That his mother would soon come back
Being the son of parents who have gone to heaven
lessons.notes: Poem by William Cowper, written on receiving his mother's portrait. The book's life sketch mentions his mental illness and suicide attempt; preview it for younger readers.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXV: Death of Samson
steps: New words: livery (a servant's uniform), timbrels (tambourines), cataphracts (soldiers in full armor), thrall (a captive slave), immixed (mixed in among)
Read Judges 16:23–30, then read Milton's account aloud
Narrate the scene as the Hebrew messenger who saw it
questions: Who tells the story of Samson's death in this passage?
What did Samson ask his guide to let him do?
Who escaped the destruction?
answers: A Hebrew who happened to be in Gaza, telling Samson's father, Manoah
Lean on the two great pillars that held up the roof, saying he was tired
Only the common people standing outside
lessons.notes: From John Milton's 'Samson Agonistes.' Milton wrote it after he had gone blind.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXVI: An Evening Adventure
steps: New words: gig (a light two-wheeled carriage), withes (flexible twigs used as ties), yeomanry (small farmers), altercation (a heated argument), sophistry (clever but false reasoning)
Read the story aloud; keep the surprise for the end
Narrate: what did the young lawyers assume about the old man, and how were they proved wrong?
questions: Why did the travelers think the old man was a plain farmer?
What were the young men arguing about?
Who turned out to be the old gentleman?
answers: His gig was mended with hickory bark and his clothes were plain and careless
The merits of the Christian religion (pulpit versus courtroom eloquence)
John Marshall, Chief Justice of the United States
lessons.notes: The author is not named in the book. A good lesson on not judging by appearances.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXVII: The Barefoot Boy
steps: New words: pantaloons (trousers), jaunty (lively, carefree), eschewing (avoiding), Hesperides (in Greek myth, keepers of the golden apples), moil (drudgery)
Read the poem aloud cheerfully
Memorize the opening lines, from “Blessings on thee, little man” to “I was once a barefoot boy!”
List five things the barefoot boy learned from nature, not from school
questions: What does the boy have that the rich man cannot buy?
Where does the boy get his knowledge?
What does the poet fear will happen to the boy's feet when he grows up?
answers: Outward sunshine and inward joy
From nature: bees, birds, flowers, berries, and animals
They will be shut in shoes and set to work in the mills of toil
lessons.notes: Poem by John Greenleaf Whittier, Quaker poet and abolitionist.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXVIII: The Glove and the Lions
steps: New words: valor (courage), ramped (reared up), smother (a thick cloud of dust), quoth (said)
Read the ballad aloud with a galloping rhythm
Narrate the story and give the king's verdict in your own words
questions: Why did the lady drop her glove among the lions?
What did the Count do with the glove?
What did King Francis say about the lady's test?
answers: To prove the Count's love and win glory for herself
Fetched it and threw it in her face
That vanity, not love, sets love a task like that
lessons.notes: Poem by Leigh Hunt. The king is Francis I of France.

lessons.title: Lesson LXXXIX: The Folly of Intoxication
steps: New words: bestial (like a beast), fustian (pompous nonsense), inordinate (excessive), importune (beg), Hydra (a many-headed monster of myth)
Read the note on Iago and Cassio, then read the scene aloud with a partner
Copywork: “Oh that men should put an enemy in their mouths to steal away their brains!”
questions: What does Cassio grieve over losing?
What advice does Iago give him?
Is Iago really Cassio's friend?
answers: His reputation
To beg Desdemona, the general's wife, to win his place back
No; he is the villain who got Cassio drunk to ruin him
lessons.notes: From Shakespeare's 'Othello,' Act II, Scene 3. Chosen for its warning against drunkenness, a frequent theme in the McGuffey Readers.

lessons.title: Lesson XC: Starved Rock
steps: New words: plummet (a weight on a line for sounding depth), palisade (a fence of stakes), timorous (fearful), cantonments (camps), aegis (protection)
Read the description aloud
Find Starved Rock on the Illinois River on a map; sketch the cliff and the valley from Parkman's words
questions: Why did La Salle choose the rock for his fort?
Whom did the Illinois tribes see La Salle as protecting them from?
How did Starved Rock get its name, according to the legend in the notes?
answers: It was steep on three sides and could be climbed only by one narrow path
The Iroquois
A band of Illinois Indians besieged there by the Potawatomi starved (or died of thirst)
lessons.notes: By Francis Parkman, the historian of French America. Some wording reflects 19th-century views of Native peoples.

lessons.title: Lesson XCI: Prince Henry and Falstaff
steps: New words: sack (a sweet wine), buckram (stiff cloth), doublet (a close-fitting jacket), strappado (an instrument of torture), extempore (made up on the spot)
Read the scene aloud with a group, one reader for Falstaff and one for the Prince
Keep a tally as Falstaff tells his story: how many 'men in buckram' does he claim?
questions: How many men in buckram does Falstaff's story grow to?
What really happened at the robbery?
What excuse does Falstaff give at the end?
answers: From two, to four, to seven, nine, and eleven
The Prince and Poins, just two, robbed the four robbers, and Falstaff ran away roaring
He knew it was the Prince and would not harm the true heir; he was 'a coward on instinct'
lessons.notes: From Shakespeare's 'Henry IV, Part 1,' Act II, Scene 4. Falstaff drinks and swears an oath that insults Jews, both of their time; worth a word.

lessons.title: Lesson XCII: Studies
steps: New words: affectation (showing off), contemn (scorn), confute (prove wrong), conference (discussion), subtle (sharp, keen)
Read the essay aloud slowly; it is packed with ideas
Copywork: “Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested.”
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain one of Bacon's sayings with an example from your own reading
questions: What are the three uses of studies?
What, says Bacon, should we read for?
What does reading make a man? conference? writing?
answers: Delight, ornament, and ability
To weigh and consider, not to contradict, believe blindly, or find talk
Reading makes a full man; conference a ready man; writing an exact man
lessons.notes: By Sir Francis Bacon, from his 'Essays.'

lessons.title: Lesson XCIII: Surrender of Granada
steps: New words: barb (a Barbary horse), ecclesiastic (a churchman), Te Deum (a hymn of praise), mien (bearing, appearance), stoical (bearing pain without complaint)
Read the notes, then read the chapter aloud; make the final scene slow
Find Granada on a map of Spain; talk about why 1492 was a turning point
questions: Who was Boabdil?
To whom did Ferdinand give the keys of Granada?
What is the place where Boabdil wept still called?
answers: The last Moorish king of Granada
Queen Isabel (Isabella)
The Last Sigh of the Moor
lessons.notes: From Bulwer-Lytton's novel 'Leila, or the Siege of Granada.' Granada fell to Spain in 1492.

lessons.title: Lesson XCIV: Hamlet's Soliloquy
steps: New words: soliloquy (a speech to oneself), consummation (an ending), contumely (insulting treatment), quietus (release, death), bourn (boundary)
Read the soliloquy aloud slowly and thoughtfully
Memorize the opening lines, to “And by opposing end them?”
questions: What question is Hamlet weighing?
What keeps people bearing their troubles rather than escaping them?
answers: Whether it is better to live and endure troubles or to die
Dread of what comes after death, 'the undiscovered country'
lessons.notes: From Shakespeare's 'Hamlet,' Act III, Scene 1. Hamlet is thinking about ending his life; be ready to talk about it with care.

lessons.title: Lesson XCV: Ginevra
steps: New words: heirloom (an object handed down in a family), coronet (a small crown), decorum (proper behavior), nuptial (of a wedding), ambush (a hidden trap)
Read the poem aloud as a traveler's tale, slowing down for the discovery
Narrate the story of Ginevra from the wedding feast to the opening of the chest
questions: What happened to Ginevra at her wedding feast?
How was the mystery solved fifty years later?
What was the 'ambush' in the chest?
answers: She vanished during a game of hide-and-seek and was never found
The old chest burst open while being moved, revealing her skeleton, jewels, and ring
A spring lock that shut her in
lessons.notes: Poem by Samuel Rogers, from 'Italy.' A sad, eerie tale based on a legend.

lessons.title: Lesson XCVI: Inventions and Discoveries
steps: New words: circumnavigated (sailed around), diffused (spread widely), ascendency (dominance), maximum (the greatest amount), impious (lacking reverence)
Read the essay aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, list the inventions Calhoun names and what each did for the world. What would he add today?
questions: What new power does Calhoun say these inventions gave rise to?
What does he credit the mariner's compass with?
Did he think inventions would end up helping or harming mankind?
answers: Public opinion, with the press as its voice
Making it possible to sail around and explore the globe and spread commerce
Helping; to doubt it would be impious
lessons.notes: By John C. Calhoun, from 'A Disquisition on Government.' Parent note: the book's sketch says plainly that Calhoun defended slavery as 'neither morally nor politically wrong.' His view that gunpowder settled the contest between 'civilization and barbarism' is also worth discussing.

lessons.title: Lesson XCVII: Enoch Arden at the Window
steps: New words: harassed (troubled), allured (drew in), shingle (beach pebbles), burnished (polished), swoon (faint)
Read the note first, then read the poem aloud quietly
