Written narration: in a paragraph, tell what Enoch saw through the window and what he decided
questions: Why had Enoch been gone so long?
Whom did Enoch see by Philip's fireside?
What did Enoch resolve as he walked home?
answers: He was shipwrecked on a lonely island and thought dead
His wife Annie, now married to Philip, their baby, and his own grown children
Never to tell her or let her know he was alive
lessons.notes: From Alfred Tennyson's 'Enoch Arden' (1864). A story of self-sacrifice; he dies soon after of a broken heart.

lessons.title: Lesson XCVIII: Lochinvar
steps: New words: dauntless (fearless), laggard (a slowpoke), craven (cowardly), galliard (a lively dance), croup (a horse's rump)
Read the ballad aloud with galloping speed
Memorize the first stanza, “Oh, young Lochinvar is come out of the west”
questions: Why did Lochinvar arrive too late?
What did he ask to do at the wedding?
How did he carry off the bride?
answers: The bride had already agreed to wed another man
Dance one dance and drink one cup of wine with the bride
He swung her onto his horse at the hall door and galloped away
lessons.notes: By Sir Walter Scott, a song from 'Marmion.'

lessons.title: Lesson XCIX: Speech on the Trial of a Murderer
steps: New words: opprobrium (disgrace, scorn), precedent (an earlier example), depravity (wickedness), bludgeon (a club), poniard (a dagger)
Read the note on the Salem case, then read the speech aloud
Copywork: “The secret which the murderer possesses soon comes to possess him.”
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain why Webster says such a secret can never be safe
questions: What made this murder different from most?
Why, says Webster, will such a crime be discovered?
What does the guilty conscience do to the murderer?
answers: It was cool and calculated, done only for pay, not anger or revenge
Thousands of eyes and minds are searching, and Providence orders that 'murder will out'
Torments him until the secret demands to be confessed
lessons.notes: By Daniel Webster, from the 1830 Salem trial for the murder of Captain Joseph White. The murder is described in detail, and the speech mentions suicide; preview it.

lessons.title: Lesson C: The Closing Year
steps: New words: knell (the toll of a funeral bell), cadences (rhythms), specter (a ghost), serried (in close ranks), blazonry (bright display)
Read the poem aloud solemnly, as at midnight on New Year's Eve
Copywork: three lines that you find most striking
questions: At what hour is the poem set?
What does the poet compare to the condor that rests at night?
answers: Midnight at the end of the year
Time, which, unlike the condor, never rests
lessons.notes: Poem by George D. Prentice, editor of the 'Louisville Journal.' A good reading for New Year's Eve.

lessons.title: Lesson CI: A New City in Colorado
steps: New words: plateau (high, flat land), gulch (a narrow ravine), apertures (openings), candelabrum (a branched candlestick), impromptu (made up on the spot)
Read the sketch aloud; let the hammers 'clink' in your voice
Narrate: describe Perry's Hotel and the 'bedrooms' in it
questions: How old was Garland City when the author arrived?
Why were houses not going up even faster?
How had the landlord moved his hotel?
answers: Twelve days old
The sawmills could not cut lumber fast enough
He took it down over his guests' heads at Wagon Creek and was putting it up again at Garland
lessons.notes: By Helen Hunt Jackson, from 'Bits of Travel at Home.' She later wrote 'A Century of Dishonor' about wrongs done to Native Americans.

lessons.title: Lesson CII: Importance of the Union
steps: New words: benign (kindly), copious (plentiful), precipice (a cliff edge), belligerent (warlike), peroration (the closing part of a speech)
Read the speech aloud, building to the final words
Memorize “Liberty and Union, now and forever, one and inseparable!” and the sentence leading up to it
questions: What does Webster say the Union grew out of?
What does he pray never to see?
What two mottoes does he reject?
answers: Hard times: disordered finances, ruined commerce, and credit
The Union broken, the states at war, the land drenched in fraternal blood
“What is all this worth?” and “Liberty first, and Union afterwards”
lessons.notes: By Daniel Webster, the close of his 1830 reply to Hayne. Thirty years later the Civil War he feared came.

lessons.title: Lesson CIII: The Influences of the Sun
steps: New words: terrestrial (of the earth), organic (living), inorganic (not living), projectile (something thrown or fired), Proteus (a sea god who could change shape)
Read the essay aloud
Written narration: trace one chain of energy from the sun to something you used today (food, a car, electricity)
questions: What two kinds of earthly power does Tyndall leave out of the sun's work?
How does the sun lift rivers to the mountains?
What is the point of the comparison with the clock?
answers: Volcanoes and tides
By evaporating water that falls as rain and snow on the heights
As a clock's power comes from the hand that wound it, all earthly power comes from the sun
lessons.notes: By John Tyndall, physicist. Accurate for its day; today we would add nuclear and geothermal energy to his exceptions.

lessons.title: Lesson CIV: Colloquial Powers of Franklin
steps: New words: colloquial (of conversation), vociferous (loud and forceful), adventitious (added from outside), coruscations (flashes of light), felicity (happy skill)
Read the essay aloud
Narrate: compare Franklin's way of talking with Dr. Johnson's, as Wirt describes them
questions: Why were Wirt and Franklin shut indoors for weeks?
How did Johnson's conversation differ from Franklin's?
How did Franklin make what he read his own?
answers: Deep, constant snows
Johnson's was a stormy contest for victory; Franklin's was plain, easy, and unaffected
He read and thought deeply and worked what he learned into something more valuable
lessons.notes: By William Wirt, U.S. Attorney General and biographer of Patrick Henry.

lessons.title: Lesson CV: The Dream of Clarence
steps: New words: inestimable (too valuable to measure), perjury (lying under oath), Furies (spirits of vengeance), requites (repays), environed (surrounded)
Read the notes on the Wars of the Roses, then read the scene aloud with a partner
Narrate Clarence's dream in three parts: the fall overboard, the sea floor, and the land of the dead
questions: Who knocked Clarence overboard in his dream?
What did he see on the bottom of the sea?
Which two spirits accused him after death?
answers: His brother Gloster (Gloucester)
Wrecks, drowned men, and gold, pearls, and jewels scattered, some in dead men's skulls
Warwick, his father-in-law, and Prince Edward, whom he stabbed at Tewkesbury
lessons.notes: From Shakespeare's 'Richard III,' Act I, Scene 4. A dark, vivid scene; Clarence is murdered shortly afterward.

lessons.title: Lesson CVI: Homeward Bound
steps: New words: taffrail (the rail at a ship's stern), halyards (ropes for raising sails), studding sail (an extra sail set beside the regular ones), knots (sea miles per hour), forecastle (the forward part of a ship)
Read the passage aloud with the energy of a ship running before a gale
Find Cape Horn and the Falkland Islands on a map; trace the ship's way home to Boston
questions: Why were the sailors so excited?
What did the mate keep saying to the ship?
How fast was the ship going at four bells?
answers: The captain turned the ship north, straight for Boston, with Cape Horn behind them
“Hurrah, old bucket! The Boston girls have got hold of the towrope!” (and 'As long as she cracks, she holds!')
Eleven knots
lessons.notes: By Richard Henry Dana Jr., from 'Two Years Before the Mast' (1840). Lots of sailing terms; enjoy them rather than define every one.

lessons.title: Lesson CVII: Impeachment of Warren Hastings
steps: New words: impeachment (a formal charge against a public official), grenadiers (elite soldiers), proconsul (a governor of a province), arraign (accuse formally), misdemeanors (wrongdoings)
Read the scene aloud; let Burke's final lines ring out
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe the trial scene as if you were in the gallery
questions: Where was Hastings tried?
Who opened the case against him, and how long did his speech take?
In whose names did Burke impeach Hastings?
answers: In Westminster Hall (the great hall of William Rufus)
Edmund Burke, over four sittings of the court
The House of Commons, the English nation, the people of India, and human nature itself
lessons.notes: By Thomas Babington Macaulay. Hastings, governor-general of British India, was acquitted in 1795 after a seven-year trial.

lessons.title: Lesson CVIII: Destruction of the Carnatic
steps: New words: convention (an agreement), incorrigible (unable to be reformed), animosities (hatreds), exigency (an emergency), decorum (good taste, propriety)
Read the notes first, then read Burke's speech aloud
Find Madras (Chennai) and the Carnatic coast on a map of India
questions: Why did Hyder Ali decide to lay waste the Carnatic?
What did British armies find when they marched through it later?
Why does Burke stop describing the famine?
answers: The East India Company's men broke every treaty and could not be trusted
Not one man, woman, child, or animal; only silence
The details were too horrible to describe with decency
lessons.notes: By Edmund Burke, 1785, blaming the East India Company's greed for this catastrophe. Strong descriptions of war and famine.

lessons.title: Lesson CIX: The Raven
steps: New words: quaint (old-fashioned and odd), surcease (an end), obeisance (a bow), Pallas (Athena, goddess of wisdom), nepenthe (a drug that eases grief)
Read the poem aloud, enjoying its rhyme and repetition; take turns by stanza
Memorize the first stanza, “Once upon a midnight dreary…”
questions: Whom is the speaker mourning?
Where does the raven perch?
What is the only word the raven says?
answers: Lenore, a lost maiden
On a bust of Pallas above his chamber door
“Nevermore”
lessons.notes: Poem by Edgar Allan Poe (1845). Moody and dark, but a favorite to read aloud.

lessons.title: Lesson CX: A View of the Colosseum
steps: New words: prostrated (laid flat), gladiatorial (of gladiators, who fought for show), amphitheater (an oval arena with rising seats), lambent (softly glowing), coronet (a small crown)
Read the description aloud
Look at a picture of the Colosseum and describe it in your own words, as Dewey did by moonlight
questions: What happened in the Colosseum's arena long ago?
What sounds did Dewey hear inside the ruin at night?
What did the moonlit Colosseum look like from outside?
answers: Gladiator fights and the martyrdom of Christians
Only bats, a distant carriage, and a convent bell
A coronet of the heavens, a crown on the brow of night
lessons.notes: By Orville Dewey, a Unitarian minister, from his travels.

lessons.title: Lesson CXI: The Bridge
steps: New words: goblet (a drinking cup), eddying (swirling), brine (salt water), encumbered (weighed down)
Read the poem aloud slowly and quietly
Copywork: “And only the sorrow of others / Throws its shadow over me.”
questions: What does the moon's reflection look like to the poet?
How have the poet's feelings changed since his younger days on the bridge?
Whom does he think of when he crosses the bridge now?
answers: A golden goblet falling and sinking into the sea
His own heavy burden is gone; only the sorrows of others shadow him now
The thousands of care-burdened people who have crossed it since, young and old
lessons.notes: Poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, about the bridge between Boston and Cambridge.

lessons.title: Lesson CXII: Objects and Limits of Science
steps: New words: opportune (well-timed), nebulae (cloudy patches of stars or gas), strata (layers of rock), Leviathan and Behemoth (great beasts described in Job), solvents (substances that dissolve)
Read the address aloud, giving each 'Let them…' its own weight
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain what Winthrop says science may freely do and where he says it must stop. Do you agree?
questions: Name three things Winthrop invites scientists to do.
Where does he say science should not go?
answers: Find new planets, track comets, forecast storms, relieve pain with ether, study rock layers and fossils (any three)
It should not try to search out God or test the mysteries of faith
lessons.notes: By Robert C. Winthrop, Speaker of the U.S. House. A 19th-century view of science and faith worth discussing.

lessons.title: Lesson CXIII: The Downfall of Poland
steps: New words: pandours and hussars (kinds of fierce soldiers), van (the front of an army), presaging (foretelling), Sarmatia (an old name for Poland's region), tocsin (an alarm bell)
Read the poem aloud with rising feeling
Memorize the last two lines, “Hope, for a season, bade the world farewell, / And Freedom shrieked as Kosciusko fell!”
questions: Who was Warsaw's last champion?
What oath did his warriors swear?
Which three powers attacked Poland, according to the notes?
answers: Kosciusko
To live for their country and die with her; 'Revenge or death'
Russia, Prussia, and Austria
lessons.notes: From Thomas Campbell's 'The Pleasures of Hope.' Kosciusko had fought for America in the Revolution.

lessons.title: Lesson CXIV: Labor
steps: New words: productive industry (work that makes useful goods), vocation (a calling, a job), buttress (a support), diversity (variety), disparity (inequality)
Read the essay aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain why Greeley says every child should learn a useful trade. What practical skill would you choose?
questions: Why does Greeley want even future lawyers and poets to learn a trade?
Why are regions with only one kind of work usually poor?
What did Webster mean by 'There is plenty of room higher up'?
answers: So they always have something to fall back on and need never compromise their honesty
One occupation cannot use the different abilities of men, women, old, young, strong, and weak
There is always work for people of real skill and ability
lessons.notes: By Horace Greeley, editor of the 'New York Tribune.' His figures and comparisons of states are from the 1800s.

lessons.title: Lesson CXV: The Last Days of Herculaneum
steps: New words: solace (comfort), fettered (chained), ominous (threatening), frenzy (wild excitement), corse (a corpse)
Read the notes first, then read the poem aloud with feeling
Find Vesuvius, Pompeii, and Herculaneum on a map of Italy
questions: Why was the soldier in a dungeon?
What had happened to the boy?
How did the father and son die?
answers: For some daring deed that broke the law
He was killed by lightning while the earth shook
The ground moved the boy's body into his arms, and the prison fell into the opening earth
lessons.notes: From Edwin Atherstone's 'The Last Days of Herculaneum.' The eruption of Vesuvius buried the city in A.D. 79. A sad and dramatic poem.

lessons.title: Lesson CXVI: How Men Reason
steps: New words: saccharine (sugary sweet), placid (calm), stringent (sharp, harsh), windfalls (fruit blown down by the wind)
Read the essay aloud in a chatty, humorous voice
Narrate: explain Holmes's comparison of people to pears
questions: Why does Holmes say he would not trust praise from a critic over fifty?
How are people like pears?
answers: Older authors tend to stop finding fault and praise everything
Some ripen early, some late; a hard, sour one may turn out to be a fine winter pear, so don't judge too quickly
lessons.notes: By Oliver Wendell Holmes, from 'The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table.'

lessons.title: Lesson CXVII: Thunderstorm on the Alps
steps: New words: placid (calm), concentered (gathered together), phosphoric (glowing), cleaves (cuts through), thwarted (blocked)
Read the notes on Lake Geneva, then read the stanzas aloud: quietly at first, then with the storm
Memorize the stanza beginning “The sky is changed!”
questions: How does the poet feel about the calm lake?
What mountains answer the Alps in the storm?
What does Byron compare the two heights split by the Rhone to?
answers: It warns him to leave earth's troubles for something purer, like a sister's gentle rebuke
The Jura
Two lovers who parted in anger and can never meet again
lessons.notes: From Lord Byron's 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage,' Canto III.

lessons.title: Lesson CXVIII: Origin of Property
steps: New words: dominion (rule, control), primeval (of the earliest times), usufructuary (having the use, but not the ownership, of a thing), sequacious (inclined to follow; tame), concomitants (things that go along with something)
Read the essay aloud in sections; stop to summarize each step
Written narration: in a paragraph, trace Blackstone's steps from shared land to private property and government
questions: What was the first kind of 'ownership' Blackstone describes?
Why did farming lead to owning land?
What Bible story does he use about sharing land?
answers: A right to use a thing only as long as one was using it, like a seat in a theater
No one would till the soil if another could seize the harvest
Abraham and Lot separating to the left and right
lessons.notes: By Sir William Blackstone, from his 'Commentaries on the Laws of England.' A challenging reading; take two sittings if needed.

lessons.title: Lesson CXIX: Battle of Waterloo
steps: New words: revelry (merrymaking), chivalry (knights; brave gentlemen), knell (a death bell), impetuous (rushing), verdure (green growth)
Read the notes, then read the stanzas aloud; change from the dance to the cannon
Memorize the first stanza, “There was a sound of revelry by night”
questions: Where were the officers when the cannon began?
What did the dancers first think the sound was?
What does the last stanza say happened in a single day?
answers: At a ball in Brussels
The wind, or a carriage rattling over the street
They went from life and dancing to battle and death, buried together, friend and foe
lessons.notes: From Lord Byron's 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.' Waterloo, June 18, 1815, ended Napoleon's rule.

lessons.title: Lesson CXX: "With Brains, Sir"
steps: New words: dilettante (a dabbler in an art), commodity (a useful thing), chiaroscuro (light and shade in a painting), aesthetics (the study of beauty)
Read the essay aloud
Copywork: “Suppose you look again.”
Try it: look at a picture or object for five minutes and write down what you see on the second look
questions: What did Opie say he mixed his colors with?
What did Etty answer when a student asked what something meant?
Why does the author think these short answers were best?
answers: “With brains, sir.”
“Suppose you look,” and then “Suppose you look again.”
They made students think and see for themselves instead of being told
lessons.notes: By Dr. John Brown, author of 'Rab and His Friends.' A favorite essay for Charlotte Mason–minded families.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXI: The New England Pastor
steps: New words: verdant (green), hallowed (holy), swains (country youths), engrossed (completely occupied), steep (a steep slope)
Read the poem aloud gently
Narrate: describe the pastor's house, his looks, and his one care
questions: How long had the pastor served?
What did his face look like, according to the poet?
What was his only care?
answers: Forty years ('twice twenty years')
Grave and wise, glowing with an 'October light,' like evening
To bless and save his people and point them to heaven
lessons.notes: From a poem by Timothy Dwight, president of Yale College and grandson of Jonathan Edwards.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXII: Death of Absalom
steps: New words: succor (help), shekels (Hebrew silver coins), tidings (news), compassed about (surrounded)
Read the chapter aloud; give David's cry at the end its full sorrow
Read 2 Samuel 15 in your Bible to learn why Absalom rebelled
questions: What order did David give his captains about Absalom?
How was Absalom caught?
Which runner told David the truth about Absalom?
answers: Deal gently with the young man for David's sake
His head caught in the branches of an oak as his mule ran on
Cushi (Ahimaaz did not say)
lessons.notes: From the Bible, 2 Samuel 18.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXIII: Abraham Davenport
steps: New words: sagas (old Norse tales), inexorable (unbending), adjourn (end a meeting), alewives (a kind of herring), self-poised (calm and balanced)
Read the note on the Dark Day, then read the poem aloud
Memorize from “Let God do his work, we will see to ours” to “Bring in the candles.”
questions: What happened on May 19, 1780?
What did some lawmakers want to do?
What business did the legislature go on with?
answers: A strange darkness covered New England at midday
Adjourn, thinking it was Judgment Day
An act to regulate the shad and alewive fisheries
lessons.notes: Poem by John Greenleaf Whittier. The Dark Day was probably caused by smoke from huge forest fires.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXIV: The Falls of the Yosemite
steps: New words: perpendicular (straight up and down), rampart (a protective wall), declivity (a downward slope), cataract (a great waterfall), serpentine (snaking)
Read the description aloud
Look up a photo of Yosemite Falls and compare it to King's description
questions: How high is the Yosemite fall, according to King?
What shape does the upper fall take as it widens?
What does the wind sometimes do to the fall?
answers: Nearly 2,500 feet, in three leaps
A comet
Gets behind it and swings or twists it like a pendulum of lace
lessons.notes: By Thomas Starr King. Yosemite Falls is in fact among the tallest in North America, though not the highest in the world as he believed.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXV: A Psalm of Life
steps: New words: numbers (lines of verse), bivouac (a temporary camp), sublime (noble, grand), forlorn (lonely, hopeless)
Read the poem aloud with energy
Memorize the whole poem over the week, a few stanzas each day
questions: What does the poet say life is NOT?
What do the lives of great men remind us?
What are the last instructions of the poem?
answers: An empty dream
That we too can make our lives noble and leave footprints on the sands of time
Be up and doing; achieve and pursue; learn to labor and to wait
lessons.notes: Poem by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, one of the most memorized poems in American schools.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXVI: Franklin's Entry into Philadelphia
steps: New words: wharf (a landing place for boats), fatigued (very tired), draught (a drink), accosting (going up to and speaking to), reputable (respectable)
Read Franklin's account aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, tell Franklin's first day in Philadelphia as if you were the young Miss Read watching from her door
questions: How much money did Franklin have when he arrived?
What did he do with the three rolls?
Where did he first fall asleep in Philadelphia?
answers: A Dutch dollar and about a shilling in copper
Ate one, carried two under his arms, then gave the other two to a woman and child from the boat
In the Quaker meetinghouse
lessons.notes: From Benjamin Franklin's 'Autobiography.' He was seventeen.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXVII: Lines to a Waterfowl
steps: New words: fowler (a bird hunter), plashy (marshy, splashy), marge (edge), illimitable (boundless), zone (a region of the earth)
Read the poem aloud, then reread the last stanza slowly
Copywork the last stanza
questions: What guides the bird along its pathless way?
What lesson does the poet take for himself?
answers: A Power (God) who cares for it
The same One who guides the bird will lead his steps aright on his own lonely way
lessons.notes: Poem by William Cullen Bryant, written when he was a young man uncertain of his future.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXVIII: Goldsmith and Addison
steps: New words: wayward (willful), truant (wandering from duty), minstrel (a traveling singer), eccentricities (odd habits), misanthrope (a hater of people)
Read both portraits aloud; read Addison's hymn verses slowly
Narrate: why, according to Thackeray, do readers love Goldsmith?
questions: Which of Goldsmith's works were based on his boyhood home of Lissoy?
What does Thackeray say our love for Goldsmith is half made of?
Whose life does he call one of the most enviable?
answers: 'The Deserted Village' (Auburn) and 'The Vicar of Wakefield'
Pity
Joseph Addison's
lessons.notes: By William Makepeace Thackeray, from 'The English Humourists of the Eighteenth Century.' The lesson has two parts, '1. Goldsmith' and 'II. Addison.'

lessons.title: Lesson CXXIX: Immortality of the Soul
steps: New words: immortality (living forever), conjectures (guesses), bane (something that destroys), antidote (a cure)
Read the soliloquy aloud slowly
Talk it over: what reasons does Cato give for believing the soul lives on?
questions: What book is Cato reading?
What does Cato call 'doubly armed'?
What will outlast the stars and the sun?
answers: Plato's book on the immortality of the soul
His sword (death) and his book (the hope of life after death)
The soul
lessons.notes: From Joseph Addison's tragedy 'Cato.' The speech comes just before Cato takes his own life; read ahead and be ready to talk about it.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXX: Character of Washington
steps: New words: benignant (kindly), apposite (fitting), affable (friendly), sagacity (wisdom), subterfuge (trickery)
Read the portrait aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, choose three of Washington's traits from Sparks and give an example of each from what you know of his life
questions: What does Sparks say was perhaps Washington's most remarkable trait?
What could Washington never forgive easily?
What was his strongest passion?
answers: Self-control
Dishonesty and trickery (subterfuge)
Love of his country
lessons.notes: By Jared Sparks, Washington's early biographer. An admiring portrait that leaves out that Washington held enslaved people; older students may want to discuss this.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXXI: Eulogy on Washington
steps: New words: eulogy (a speech of praise for the dead), compeer (an equal, companion), despondency (low spirits), effulgence (radiance)
Read the notes on the battles, then deliver the eulogy aloud
Memorize “First in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen.”
questions: Who gave this eulogy, and when?
Whom did Washington bring to surrender at the end of the war?
How did Washington face his death?
answers: General Henry ('Light-Horse Harry') Lee, at Congress's request in 1799
Cornwallis, at Yorktown
With calm serenity; not a sigh or groan despite great pain
lessons.notes: By Henry Lee, father of Robert E. Lee.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXXII: The Solitary Reaper
steps: New words: solitary (alone), vale (valley), plaintive (sad, mournful), Hebrides (islands off western Scotland), lay (a song)
Read the poem aloud softly
Memorize the last four lines, from “I listened motionless and still”
questions: What is the Highland girl doing as she sings?
Why can the poet not understand her song?
What did he carry away with him?
answers: Reaping and binding grain alone in the field
She sings in Gaelic, a language he does not know
The music in his heart, long after he could no longer hear it
lessons.notes: Poem by William Wordsworth, written after a walking tour in Scotland.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXXIII: Value of the Present
steps: New words: aliment (food, nourishment), illusory (deceptive), dupe (one who is fooled), dizened (dressed up showily), bivouacs (camps out)
Read the essay aloud slowly; Emerson packs a thought into every sentence
Copywork: “Write it on your heart that every day is the best day in the year.”
Written narration: in a paragraph, explain Emerson's idea that the gods 'come in low disguises,' using his examples
questions: What illusion, says Emerson, hides the value of the present hour?
Name two examples he gives of greatness hidden in humble form.
What did Bonaparte say about a general's troops?
answers: That the present hour is not the important, decisive one; we always think we are doing something less than our best task
Odin in a fisher's hut, Apollo with shepherds, Jesus born in a barn with fishermen for friends (any two)
A general always has troops enough if he knows how to use the ones he has
lessons.notes: By Ralph Waldo Emerson, from 'Works and Days.' One of the hardest readings in the book; read it in two sittings if needed.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXXIV: Happiness
steps: New words: competence (enough to live on), temperance (self-control), prunella (a cloth used for shoes), huzzas (cheers)
Read the verses aloud, pausing at each couplet
Memorize “Honor and shame from no condition rise; / Act well your part, there all the honor lies.”
questions: In what three words does Pope say happiness lies?
Does God change his laws for good people, according to Pope?
What does Pope call 'the noblest work of God'?
answers: Health, peace, and competence
No; gravitation does not stop for a good man passing under a falling rock
An honest man
lessons.notes: From Alexander Pope's 'Essay on Man.' The book's sketch of Pope's character is frank.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXXV: Marion
steps: New words: impregnable (unconquerable), partisan (a guerrilla fighter), circumspection (caution), fords (shallow river crossings), privation (hardship, want)
Read the description aloud
Written narration: in a paragraph, describe how Marion kept his plans secret and how his men guessed them
questions: What served as Marion's moat and walls?
Why did Marion prefer fords to bridges?
How did his men know a long march was coming?
answers: The swamp was his moat and the deep ravines his walls
Bridges helped the enemy and warned them he was coming
They watched his cook preparing extra portable food; and he usually set out at sunset
lessons.notes: By William Gilmore Simms, from 'The Life of Francis Marion,' the 'Swamp Fox' of the Revolution. See also Lesson LXX.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXXVI: A Common Thought
steps: New words: solemn (serious, grave), musky (heavy-scented), zenith (the highest point of the sky)
Read the poem aloud slowly
Talk it over: why might the book's editors call this poem almost a prophecy?
questions: What 'solemn day' is the poet thinking of?
At what time of day does he imagine his death?
answers: The day of his own death
At dawn, as the day breaks
lessons.notes: Poem by Henry Timrod, the South Carolina poet, who died young in poverty after the Civil War, much as the poem imagines. A brief poem about death.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXXVII: A Definite Aim in Reading
steps: New words: definite (clear, exact), affinity (natural attraction), omnivorous (taking in everything), indiscriminate (without choosing), nucleus (a center)
Read the essay aloud
Make a plan: choose one subject and list three or four different kinds of books (history, story, diary, poem) you could read about it
Written narration: in a paragraph, give Porter's main rules for reading and say which one you will try
questions: What question does Porter say we should often ask ourselves?
Why do self-educated readers often do better than others?
What is the 'iron in the fire' rule?
answers: “Why am I reading this, and why now?”
They know what they are reading for and choose books with a purpose
Always have one solid book in hand that you carry forward every day until finished
lessons.notes: By Noah Porter, president of Yale, from 'Books and Reading.' A natural fit for a family that reads living books.

lessons.title: Lesson CXXXVIII: Ode to Mt. Blanc
steps: New words: sovran (sovereign, supreme), ebon (black), invulnerable (unable to be harmed), hierarch (a chief priest), incense (sweet smoke offered in worship)
Read the hymn aloud, building to the great answer “God!”
Find Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps, on a map
Memorize the last line, “Earth, with her thousand voices, praises God.”
questions: What questions does the poet ask the mountain, the torrents, and the icefalls?
What answer does he want all of nature to give?
What does he ask the mountain to tell the sky, stars, and sun?
answers: Who made them, gave them their strength, light, and beauty
God!
That Earth, with her thousand voices, praises God
lessons.notes: By Samuel Taylor Coleridge ('Hymn Before Sunrise, in the Vale of Chamouni'). The last selection in the book; a fitting close to the year.
